blocks.text: ...means being able to let go
Leash training is not an isolated exercise programme but a training that accompanies everyday life. It takes place all the time – on every walk, in every encounter.
Collar and harness are primarily means of transmitting information and are not intended for holding the dog. The leash communicates – it does not force.
Loose-leash walking is the product of relaxation and security.
The right leash 🦮
A lead should ideally be 2 metres long, but by no means shorter than 1.20 metres.
A simple leash without buckles and fittings guarantees stress-free work.
Make sure it has a sturdy carabiner clip.
Unsuitable equipment ⚠️
A flexible, retractable leash is, by all experience, very unsuitable for general training.
Poop bag dispensers and other “clutter” have no place on the leash.
Collar or harness? 🔖
Whether a collar or a harness is used is up to each person to decide – and ultimately up to the dog.
Collar and harness are primarily means of transmitting information and are ultimately not intended for holding the dog.
The leading side 🧭
The dog is always led on the same side. Exceptions should be rare.
Do not worry about leading on the left – dogs still learn without any problem to run on the right beside a bicycle.
Getting used to walking on one side should happen continuously and calmly.
Leash handling & pace ⏱️
The leash is held mainly near its end, or at least long enough that it hangs slack and loose.
As an exception, the leash may be shortened if uninvolved people could otherwise be disturbed or endangered, or if the individual exercise requires it.
We walk at a calm pace, always slightly slower than the dog would like to go.
A good leash pace is one that brings the dog to walk at a normal gait. Trotting or even galloping pace hinders learning success.
Route choice & communication 🗣️
We preferably walk in the middle of the path to draw the dog away from the distracting edges of the path.
We walk in such a way that we radiate calmness in every respect.
We speak calmly and normally not in a commanding tone.
We praise the dog in a calm voice and stroke it soothingly.
The core of leash training is a simple but effective system with two imaginary semicircles on your leading side:
Outer circle: Within a radius of the leash length of about 2 metres
Inner circle: At a radius of approximately 1 metre, bounded by the leading side
Behaviour in the inner circle ✅
If the dog moves in the inner circle while walking, we address it from time to time in a calm, praising voice.
Every now and then we let it sit and praise it calmly.
Those who wish may give the dog a treat as a reward. However, the dog must absolutely look at us for this – otherwise it gets nothing.
Alternatively, for dogs with play drive, a toy can occasionally be produced by surprise as a short reward instead of a treat.
Correction when leaving the leading side ⚠️
If the dog leaves the leading side while walking, it is simply guided back to the correct side while walking, or during 3 to 4 steps backwards.
Over time it will get used to walking on the desired side.
What matters is the steady correction towards the chosen side.
Correction in the outer circle ⚠️

If the dog moves into the outer circle while walking (towards 2 metres of leash length), we should initiate the correction procedure. With the leash held long, we briskly walk a few steps backwards and begin to speak in a praising tone as soon as the dog follows, approaching us.
We then let it sit in front of us, facing us and looking at us, or later also go down.
Now we wait until it settles and looks at us again. This may also be supported by calmly addressing it by name.
After bringing it from the down into the sit if necessary, we praise the dog with calm stroking, calm talking and, if appropriate, with a treat or with play using a toy.
Remember: Leash work always takes place. It accompanies everyday life and is therefore essential. Leash work is thus predominantly an accompanying training.
Phase 1 – Start & basic posture 🟢
We hold the leash fairly loose and walk calmly.
Any kind of walking too fast puts the dog into a forward drive, which in turn promotes pulling on the leash.
We only set off again when the dog is in a relaxed sitting position.

We set off each time without addressing the dog. Regularly addressing the dog to start walking could take on the effect of a start signal and thus, under some circumstances, an undesired effect. Anyone who still wants to address the dog when setting off should do so in a calm and relaxed tone of voice.
Phase 2 – Building in pauses ⏸️
After a short pause, we each time calmly start anew from the sit and continue our walk.
We set off calmly with the leash held loose and long.
Phase 3 – The two options 🔀
Now our dog has two options:
It stays in the inner ‘loose’ circle – everything remains fine. We radiate calm and do not walk too fast.
Or it strives away from us into the outer circle and must again go into the ‘sit’ or also the ‘down’ as described before.
Phase 4 – Progressive improvement 📈
This process repeats itself more or less often, depending on need.
Since our untrained dog will still break away quite frequently, it is advisable at the beginning to correct only the strongly excessive behaviours.
As improvement progresses, smaller inaccuracies can then increasingly be trained as well.
Strong pulling on the leash should be corrected first – later also still slight pulling.
Controlling sniffing at the path edge ⚠️
Frequent and intense sniffing at the path edge should be consistently reduced.
Do not additionally stop or even give in to the dog, but simply keep walking on with the dog.
Do not walk near the path edge in the first place.
Consequences of strong sniffing at the path edge ⚠️

Remember: As the growing dog gets older, strong sniffing at the path edge tends to lead to a strong territorial claim and thus, possibly, to a readiness for conflict in dog encounters, combined with reduced willingness to be led.
Situational adjustment 🧠
It should be noted that our dog is not a machine and, like us, is subject to environmental influences.
Therefore always weigh up with feeling and reason whether a behaviour should be corrected.
As a general rule, we may only carry out those corrections which, given the situation, we can also bring to a positive end and thus to learning success.
Leash training should always be carried out with a relaxed presence, great composure, calm and warmth. Our dog should feel comfortable in our presence.
Behaviours to avoid ⚠️
Absolutely avoid a permanently taut leash.
Avoid a permanently short leash or a short leash in stressful situations.
Avoid the dog changing sides.
Avoid permanent sniffing at the path edge.
Avoid self-extending leashes during the learning phase, because they teach the dog that it can do as it pleases.
Avoid running after the dog or letting it pull you around at will.
Avoid uncontrolled pulling influences.
Avoid waiting for the dog when it has become fixated on sniffing somewhere.
Avoid the dog biting the leash.
Avoid everything that lets the leash act permanently taut on the dog.
Practical impulse: The “two-minute pause”

On your next walk, consciously stop three times: have your dog sit, wait for eye contact and only continue on your way once calm has set in. These short interruptions train impulse control and orientation towards you – mentally more valuable than simply walking on.
Was the dog always led on the same side?
Was the leash always held long and loose?
Did I always walk at a calm pace?
Did I walk mostly in the middle of the path?
Did I observe calm communication with the dog?
Was I harmonious and attentive?
Did I pay attention to pauses?
Was the praise calm and warm?
Did I make sure the exercise was carried out facing us?
Did I convey the inner and outer circle well to the dog?
Did I avoid adapting to the dog's pace?
Did I make sure of a pleasant training atmosphere?
